lesson.title: Centre and outliers

lead.text: Back to the five friends and their receipts. To give one number for what each person spent, we need a value that stands in for the whole list. A number like that is a measure of the list's centre, and there is more than one way to find it.

The first way is to settle up fairly. Put all the money into one pot and share it back out, so that everyone ends with the same amount. Suppose three of the friends spent £3, £5 and £10. The pot holds £18, and shared three ways it comes to £6 each. That share is the mean: add up all the values, then divide by how many there are.

The mean uses every value in the list, so each one pulls on it. The £10 drags the mean up to £6, even though two of the three friends spent less. In everyday speech this is the average, though there are other kinds of average, which is why statisticians use the more exact name.
Use the sharing idea from the last screen on five friends instead of three.
The mean needs every number in the list. A second centre uses only their order. Put the values in order, smallest first. The one in the middle is the median.

Take the list 7, 2, 9, 4 and 5. In order it reads 2, 4, 5, 7, 9. There are five values, so the middle is the third one, with two values below it and two above. The median is 5. The order matters: the middle of the list as written is a 9, which is not the middle in size.

This makes the median a different kind of centre. It cares about where a value sits in the order and ignores how far the values lie from each other. Later in the lesson we will see what that does when one value is far from the rest.
Put these values in size order first, then pick out the middle one.

With five values there is one in the middle. With four there is not. Two values sit in the middle, with one value on each side of the pair. The median then falls halfway between them, so we take their average: add the pair and halve the total.

Take 3, 9, 5 and 7. In order they read 3, 5, 7, 9. The middle pair is 5 and 7. They add to 12, and half of 12 is 6. The median is 6. It is not one of the values in the list, which is fine, because it only has to sit between them.

afterFigure.text: The same two moves work for any list. Sort it, find the middle position, and if there are two middle values, average them.

workedSteps.text: Four values have two in the middle: the second and third. Add them.
Halve that total to average the pair.

lead.text: Now for the question this lesson has been heading towards. Take the list 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. Its mean is 3 and its median is 3. Let the last value grow while the others stay put. Use the slider under the picture to drag it upwards and watch the two centres.

afterFigure.text: Drag the 5 up to 50. The total grows by 45, so the mean grows by 9, from 3 to 12, which is higher than every other value in the list. The median is still the third value in order, and the third value has not moved, so it stays at 3.
A value that sits far from the rest of the list is an outlier. The mean follows an outlier because it uses every value. The median barely notices one, because it only looks at the order.

lead.text: The list is 2, 4, 4, 5 and 25, and the 25 is an outlier. Put the values in order and find the middle.

Which centre should you quote? It depends on what the number is for. If you want to share a total out evenly, the mean is the right one, because the total is what matters and every value should count.

If you want the typical value and the list has an outlier, the median usually describes it better. Take the yearly pay in a small firm, in thousands of pounds: 20, 22, 25, 26 and 107. The mean is 40, which is more than four of the five people earn, because one high salary drags it up. The median is 25, which is close to what most of them earn.
When a mean and a median are far apart, it is a sign that something in the list is pulling at one of them.
An estate agent wants the typical price from five recent sales, and one of them was a mansion. Choose the centre that the mansion cannot skew.

reveal.text: The median stays with the ordinary houses. The mean would have been dragged upwards by the mansion.

lesson.orientation: Calculate the mean and median, and see how one extreme observation changes them differently.
lesson.nextAction: Try a new case and return for recall after a delay.

blocks.text: Five friends come back from a weekend away with a pile of receipts. One of them wants to say, in a single number for the group chat, how much each person typically spent. Everyone spent a different amount, so the number has to stand in for all of them.

There is more than one sensible way to pick it. The two most common give the same answer for some lists and quite different answers for others. When a list contains one value far from the rest, such as a single mansion among the houses on a street, the two answers drift apart and the choice starts to matter.
This lesson works out both with small lists you can do in your head. Then it moves one value around and watches what each one does.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the mean and median of a list, and say which one a single extreme value moves.

recap.keyIdea: The mean is the total shared equally and uses every value. The median is the middle of the sorted list. An outlier drags the mean and barely moves the median.

blocks.text: You shared £20 among five friends and found a mean of £4. You sorted lists to find their medians, averaging the middle pair when the count was even. With the 25 in the list 2, 4, 4, 5, 25 the mean was 8 and the median stayed at 4.

recap.nextHook: A centre says where a list sits but not how tightly its values cluster. The next lesson starts with two buses that are both 10 minutes late on average and are very different to wait for.

questions.prompt: The last 5 becomes 25, so the values are 2, 4, 4, 5 and 25. What happens to the mean and the median?
hints: Compare the total with the position of the middle value.

acceptedIdeas: The mean rises and the median stays 4
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Replacing 5 with 25 increases the total and hence the mean. The sorted middle observation is still 4, so the median is unchanged.

choices.label: The mean rises and the median stays 4

questions.onCorrect: The mean uses every value, so it rises. The median only needs the order, so it stays.

misconceptions.feedback: The total changes when one value changes, so the mean cannot stay put.
The median is a place in the sorted list, not the biggest value.

questions.prompt: Five friends have £2, £4, £4, £5 and £5. They pool the money and share it out equally. How much does each get?
hints: Add all five values, then divide by five.
There are five observations, including repeated values.
Divide the sum of all observations by their count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The total is 20 across five observations, so the mean is 20/5 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: £4. Sharing the total equally is the mean: add everything, divide by how many.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole pot. Share it among the five friends.
That averages just two of the amounts. Pool the whole pot, then share it equally.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 2, 4, 4, 5 and 25?
hints: Find the middle position after sorting.
An odd-sized sorted dataset has a single middle position.
With five values, take the third value of the sorted list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The five sorted values have 4 in the third, middle position.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The 25 is the last value in order, so the middle is untouched.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean, which the 25 drags up. The median is the middle value.
That is the largest value. The median is the middle one in size order.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 10, 2, 6 and 4?
hints: Average the middle pair, not the endpoints.
The even-sized sorted list has two middle positions.
Take the average of the second and third values, 4 and 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The middle pair is 4 and 6; its average is (4 + 6)/2 = 5.

questions.onCorrect: 5. Sort, then average the middle pair: (4 + 6) ÷ 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean. The median averages only the middle pair.
Four values have two middle ones. Combine them.

questions.prompt: What is the mean of 1, 3, 3, 5 and 18?
hints: Every observation contributes to the total.
There are five values, so the denominator is five.
Add 1 + 3 + 3 + 5 + 18 and divide the sum by five.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The total is 30, so the mean is 30/5 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. The total is 30, shared over 5 values. The 18 pulls the mean up.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the middle value, the median. The mean uses every value.
That is the total. Share it among the values.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the median is accurate?
hints: An even-sized dataset has two middle positions.

acceptedIdeas: For an even count it averages the two sorted middle values
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sort the data before locating its centre. With an even count, the median is the average of the two middle observations and need not itself be observed.

choices.label: It is always an observed value
It is always the largest value
For an even count it averages the two sorted middle values

questions.onCorrect: Sort first. With an even count, average the two middle values.

misconceptions.feedback: With an even count the middle falls between two values, so the median need not be one of them.
The largest value is the maximum. The median sits in the middle.

questions.prompt: Why sort the values before picking the middle one?
hints: Is the middle of the list as written the middle in size?

acceptedIdeas: The middle means the middle in size, not in the order written
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The median is the middle in size order. The order the values were written down tells you nothing about that.

choices.label: The middle means the middle in size, not in the order written
The mean needs the values in order

questions.onCorrect: The median is the middle in size order, so the list must be in that order first.

misconceptions.feedback: Sorting only puts the values in order. It doesn't change them.
The mean doesn't depend on order. It is only the median that does.

questions.prompt: What is the sum of the two middle values, 4 and 6? Write the number.
hints: Which two values are the middle pair of four?
Add the second value and the third.
Add the two middle values only.
questions.onCorrect: 10. The median of an even list starts from the middle pair's total.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds all four values. Only the middle pair goes in.

questions.prompt: Five houses sell for these prices, in thousands of pounds: 180, 190, 200, 210 and 720. What is the median price, in thousands?
hints: Are the prices in order? Which is in the middle?
Five values: the middle is the third.
The third price in order is the one you want.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Sorted already; the third of five is 200.

questions.onCorrect: 200. The 720 sits at the end of the list and cannot move the middle.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean, which the 720 drags up. The median is the middle price.
That is the largest price. The median is the middle one in size order.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 1, 3, 3, 5 and 18?
hints: Are the values in order?
Five values: which position is the middle?
Take the third value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The third of five sorted values is 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Compare it with the mean of 6: the 18 drags the mean and leaves the median.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean, which uses every value. The median is the middle one.
That is the largest value. The median is the middle in size order.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 1, 2 and 9?
hints: Is the list in order?
Three values: which position is the middle?
Take the middle value of the sorted list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sorted middle of three values is 2.

questions.onCorrect: The middle of the sorted list. The 9 does not move it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean, which the 9 drags up. The median is the middle value.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 8, 2, 9, 4 and 3?
hints: Put the values in order first. Which is smallest?
Five values, so the middle is the third once they are in order.
Write them from smallest to largest, then count along to the third place.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: In order the values are 2, 3, 4, 8, 9. The third of five is 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Sort first: the middle of the list as written is a 9, but the middle in size is 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the middle of the list as written. The median is the middle once the values are in size order.
That is the mean, which uses every value. The median is the middle one in order.
